extracted.intended_audience: citizens, lawmakers, and political thinkers concerned with rights, constitutions, and legitimate government
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive enumeration of the natural rights of men and citizens and accompanying political principles intended to guide constitution-making, law, and legitimate government. Includes articles (1–17) plus observations and argumentation on government legitimacy, hereditary succession, law, and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article One - Equality of Men in Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are born, and always continue, free and equal in respect of their Rights. Civil distinctions, therefore, can be founded only on Public Utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes equality as fundamental; any civil distinctions must be justified by public utility rather than birth or hereditary privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Two - Purpose of Political Associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of all Political associations is the Preservation of the Natural and Imprescriptible Rights of Man; and these rights are Liberty, Property, Security, and Resistance of Oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the goal by naming the core natural rights that government should protect: liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Three - Sovereignty of the Nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nation is essentially the source of all Sovereignty; nor can any individual, or any body of Men, be entitled to any authority which is not expressly derived from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority must be derived from the nation (the people); no extraneous or hereditary source of legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Four - Political Liberty and Its Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Liberty consists in the power of doing whatever does not Injure another. The exercise of the Natural Rights of every Man, has no other limits than those which are necessary to secure to every other Man the Free exercise of the same Rights; and these limits are determinable only by the Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty is bounded only by what protects others' equal liberties; determination of limits is a legal, not arbitrary, function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Five - Law Should Forbid Only Socially Harmful Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law ought to Prohibit only actions hurtful to Society. What is not Prohibited by the Law should not be hindered; nor should anyone be compelled to that which the Law does not Require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative liberty principle: absence of prohibition equals permissibility; law should not coerce beyond clearly harmful acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Six - Law as Expression of the Community's Will
rubrics_metrics.description: the Law is an expression of the Will of the Community. All Citizens have a right to concur, either personally or by their Representatives, in its formation. It Should be the same to all, whether it protects or punishes; and all being equal in its sight, are equally eligible to all Honours, Places, and employments, according to their different abilities, without any other distinction than that created by their Virtues and talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must be participatory (directly or via representatives), general/equal in application, and offices/ honours allocated by merit, not birth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Seven - Lawful Arrest and Protection Against Arbitrary Detention
rubrics_metrics.description: No Man should be accused, arrested, or held in confinement, except in cases determined by the Law, and according to the forms which it has prescribed. All who promote, solicit, execute, or cause to be executed, arbitrary orders, ought to be punished, and every Citizen called upon, or apprehended by virtue of the Law, ought immediately to obey, and renders himself culpable by resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest/detention require statutory basis and due procedure; arbitrary orders are punishable; citizens must obey lawful orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Eight - Legality and Proportionality of Penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law ought to impose no other penalties but such as are absolutely and evidently necessary; and no one ought to be punished, but in virtue of a Law promulgated before the offence, and Legally applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties must be necessary, proportionate, and only under pre-existing laws (no ex post facto punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Nine - Presumption of Innocence and Humane Detention
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Man being presumed innocent till he has been convicted, whenever his detention becomes indispensable, all rigour to him, more than is necessary to secure his person, ought to be provided against by the Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms presumption of innocence; detention conditions must be no harsher than necessary to secure the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Ten - Freedom of Opinion with Public Order Limit
rubrics_metrics.description: No Man ought to be molested on account of his opinions, not even on account of his Religious opinions, provided his avowal of them does not disturb the Public Order established by the Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects freedom of conscience and opinion subject to legal public-order limits. (Commentary on page questions whether this sufficiently guarantees religion and notes risk of making religion a subject of human law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Eleven - Freedom of Expression with Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The unrestrained communication of thoughts and opinions being one of the Most Precious Rights of Man, every Citizen may speak, write, and publish freely, provided he is responsible for the abuse of this Liberty, in cases determined by the Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong free-speech protection coupled with legal accountability for abuses as defined by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Twelve - Public Force for Community Benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: A Public force being necessary to give security to the Rights of Men and of Citizens, that force is instituted for the benefit of the Community and not for the particular benefit of the persons to whom it is intrusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security forces must serve public interest, not personal interests of those who command them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Thirteen - Taxation According to Ability
rubrics_metrics.description: A common contribution being necessary for the support of the Public force, and for defraying the other expenses of Government, it ought to be divided equally among the Members of the Community, according to their abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes (public contributions) should be levied equitably according to taxpayers' ability to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Fourteen - Citizen Voice in Public Contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: every Citizen has a Right, either by himself or his Representative, to a free voice in determining the necessity of Public Contributions, the appropriation of them, and their amount, mode of assessment, and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxation and public spending decisions require citizen participation (direct or representative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Fifteen - Right to Account from Public Agents
rubrics_metrics.description: every Community has a Right to demand of all its agents an account of their conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government officials must be accountable; communities can demand explanations and accounts of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Sixteen - Need for Constitution where Powers Not Separated
rubrics_metrics.description: every Community in which a Separation of Powers and a Security of Rights is not Provided for, wants a Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of powers and explicit security of rights are constitutional necessities; absence indicates need for a constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Seventeen - Inviolability of Property and Conditions for Expropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Right to Property being inviolable and sacred, no one ought to be deprived of it, except in cases of evident Public necessity, legally ascertained, and on condition of a previous just Indemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property may only be expropriated for clearly established public necessity, under legal process, and with prior fair compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational Principle - Ignorance, Neglect, or Contempt of Rights Cause Public Misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance, neglect, or contempt of human rights, are the sole causes of public misfortunes and corruptions of Government; therefore a declaration of rights is necessary to keep members attentive to rights and duties and to compare acts of government with political ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification for publishing a Declaration of Rights: to inform public and provide a standard against which legislative and executive acts can be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation - First Three Articles as Basis of Liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The first three articles comprehend in general terms the whole of a Declaration of Rights; the 4th, 5th, and 6th define more particularly what is only generally expressed in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive hierarchy: establish foundational principles (equality, ends of political association, sovereignty) then derive specific legal/political rules from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation - Declaration of Rights Implies Declaration of Duties
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Declaration of Rights was before the National Assembly some of its members remarked that if a declaration of rights were published it should be accompanied by a Declaration of Duties... A Declaration of Rights is, by reciprocity, a Declaration of Duties also. Whatever is my right as a man is also the right of another; and it becomes my duty to guarantee as well as to possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights and duties are reciprocal; drafting a declaration should recognize duties corresponding to rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle - Law Must Be Comparable to Political Ends
rubrics_metrics.description: That the acts of the legislative and executive powers of Government, being capable of being every moment compared with the end of political institutions, may be more respected; and also, that the future claims of the citizens, being directed by simple and incontestable principles, may always tend to the maintenance of the Constitution, and the general happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and executive acts should be continually evaluated against the declared ends of political institutions (preserving rights) to ensure legitimacy and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle - No Authority Except by Consent; Parliaments Are Delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of a Parliament is only a right in trust, a right by delegation, and that but from a very small part of the Nation;... The right of the Nation is an original right, as universal as taxation. The nation is the paymaster of everything, and everything must conform to its general will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes delegated representative authority from original national sovereignty; emphasizes nation’s ultimate authority and right to change form of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle - Hereditary Succession and Hereditary Rights Are Illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary succession, and hereditary rights (as they are called), can make no part of [government], because it is impossible to make wisdom hereditary... It precludes the consent of the succeeding generations; and the preclusion of consent is despotism. The rights of men in society, are neither devisable or transferable, nor annihilable, but are descendable only, and it is not in the power of any generation to intercept finally, and cut off the descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary government is criticised as usurpation and despotism; legitimate government cannot bind future generations by a will or testament that bequeaths governmental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument Against Monopoly-of-Wisdom Justification for Government
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutation of the claim that government is a 'monopoly of wisdom' and that the nation must accept wisdom-as-government; such a doctrine justifies arbitrary power and lacks origin and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects elite-aristocratic claims that only a privileged class possesses the right wisdom to govern; warns against accepting 'political reason' as cover for arbitrary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Observation - Avoid Vindictive Government Reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Assembly neither pursued those fugitive conspirators, nor took any notice of them, nor sought to retaliate in any shape whatever. Occupied with establishing a constitution founded on the Rights of Man and the Authority of the People, the only authority on which Government has a right to exist in any country, the National Assembly felt none of those mean passions which mark the character of impertinent governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on revolutionary or constitutional conduct: prioritize establishing rights and constitution over vindictive reprisals; respect popular authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution - Religion and Legal Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary questions whether Article Ten sufficiently guarantees religious right and notes that making religion a subject of human laws 'takes off from the divine dignity of religion, and weakens its operative force upon the mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting guarantees for religious liberty, consider tensions between legal regulation and the transcendent/dignified character of religion; beware of diminishing its moral force by over-legalization.
